feedback: If two intervals share an endpoint without inequality notation (e.g. 0-10 and 10-20), ask where exactly 10 goes; switch to 0≤t<10, 10≤t<20 so it settles into one class.
If any value falls in no class, your intervals have a gap — extend or adjust them so they cover the whole range without gaps.

If you join categorical bars with a line, point out the line implies an order and continuous change between categories that do not exist; grouped continuous data suits touching bars/histogram (or a frequency polygon plotted at class midpoints), and categorical data suits a bar chart with gaps.
For a pie chart, if the sectors do not sum to 360°, recheck each angle as (frequency ÷ total) × 360° rather than 360° ÷ frequency.
activities.intendedInsight: Boundary ambiguity is resolved by inequality notation so every value belongs to exactly one class; and the chart must match the data type — a line joining categorical bars implies an order and continuous change between categories that do not exist, whereas grouped continuous data is shown with touching bars (a frequency polygon through class midpoints is a separate, legitimate display for grouped continuous data).
learnerActions: Take a strip of raw running times (e.g. 30 runners' times to the nearest second) and set your own class-interval boundaries so the intervals are equal, non-overlapping and gap-free and cover the whole range.
Place each raw value into exactly one class; deliberately try writing intervals as 0-10 and 10-20, then find where a runner who took exactly 10 seconds goes — notice the ambiguity.
Rewrite the intervals using inequality notation (0≤t<10, 10≤t<20…) and confirm the boundary value now has exactly one home.
Choose which chart suits this data — bar chart, pie chart, line graph or histogram-style touching bars — then draw it and check the drawing against the data type.
If you choose a pie chart, compute each sector angle as (frequency ÷ total) × 360° and check the angles sum to 360°.
activities.title: Grouped-table-and-chart workshop (set intervals, then choose a chart)

feedback: If your frequencies do not sum to the number of data items, recount the tallies for the disputed rows.
If a value seems to belong to two class rows, your intervals overlap — fix them with inequality notation so each value lands in exactly one class.
activities.intendedInsight: Tallying keeps counting accurate and reliable; frequencies should reconcile with the total, catching miscounts.
learnerActions: Take a set of raw data (e.g. favourite sports of a class, or heights measured to the nearest cm) and count each value into its row using tally marks.
Convert the tallies to frequencies and check the frequencies sum to the total number of data points.
For continuous or wide-ranging numerical data, group into equal class intervals in inequality notation before tallying.
activities.title: Count raw data into a frequency table with tallies

feedback: If you pick a line graph for favourite sports, note that categories have no ordering or continuity to join; a bar chart or pie chart fits categorical data.
If you report only one class's value when asked to compare, cite both data sets first, then state the difference as your conclusion.
When naming the modal class, pick the interval with the highest frequency, not the highest boundary number.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing a display is a judgement driven by data type, and interpreting a comparative chart means concluding about the difference between data sets, not reading a single value.
learnerActions: Sort several data sets by which display suits them: categorical → bar chart or pie chart; grouped continuous → touching bars/histogram; proportions of a whole → pie chart; genuine time-series → line graph.
For a categorical case (e.g. pupils' favourite sports), decide whether a line graph would be a good choice and explain why or why not.
Read a bar chart comparing Class A and Class B and state a CONCLUSION about the difference between the two data sets, citing both, not just one bar's value.
Given a grouped frequency table, name the modal class (the interval with the highest frequency).
activities.title: Which chart fits? Decide, justify, and interpret comparatively
